strengths: Novel and interpretable framing of multimodal RLVR through token-level 'visual dependency,' operationalized via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on original vs. masked images.
Two well-motivated empirical insights (sparsity of visually-dependent tokens; heterogeneity of trajectory-level visual grounding) that directly justify the proposed method rather than being post-hoc.
VPPO is simple and modular—can be plugged into GRPO/DAPO—with a clear dual mechanism (trajectory-level advantage shaping + token-level gradient filtering).

Extensive empirical validation across eight diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B, 32B), with consistent and often substantial gains over strong open-source RL-tuned baselines.

Thorough ablation studies covering masking strategy, dependency metric choice (KL vs JSD vs Top-1 drop), entropy penalty, rollout group size, filtering ratio k, and shaping range, which support the design choices.

Comparison against entropy-based pivotal token selection (a natural competing baseline from text-only LLM literature) strengthens the case that visual dependency is a more suitable signal for multimodal settings.
Qualitative case studies are illustrative and show plausible correction of baseline reasoning errors.
weaknesses: The theoretical variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 3.1) relies on several strong, somewhat unrealistic assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, independence of advantage/shaping factor from gradients, second-moment dominance) and reads more as a heuristic justification than a rigorous guarantee; its practical relevance is unclear.

Computing token visual dependency requires an additional forward pass with masked images for every token in every rollout trajectory, which is a non-trivial overhead; the reported ~10% wall-clock increase is not fully substantiated with memory/compute analysis, and details of how masked-image distributions are efficiently obtained during rollout are sparse.

Baseline comparisons mix reproduced numbers (with author-provided prompts) and numbers taken directly from other papers (e.g., PAPO-D), raising potential concerns about strict comparability/fairness across methods under a single evaluation pipeline.

The ablation in Table 2 shows that combining TAS+TGF is not uniformly better than TGF alone (e.g., worse on DynaMath, Geo3k, MathVision, LogicVista), which somewhat undercuts the claimed 'synergistic value' of the hierarchical design.

No variance/seed information is reported for training runs, despite RL training being known to be sensitive to seed and initialization; only avg@8 at inference is reported, which addresses evaluation stochasticity but not training variance.
Key hyperparameters (k=0.4, β range) appear tuned on the same benchmark suite used for final evaluation, raising a mild risk of overfitting to the specific benchmark distribution.

The visual dependency metric could be confounded by token position or generic distributional sensitivity to any perturbation (not necessarily reasoning-relevant), and this potential confound is not explicitly ruled out.

The second core insight (that trajectories vary in visual groundedness) is somewhat expected/intuitive, and the main technical novelty resides primarily in the specific token-level scoring and its integration into the RL objective.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually interesting and underexplored lens for multimodal RLVR -- quantifying token-level visual dependency via KL divergence between policy outputs conditioned on original vs. masked images -- which is a reasonable attempt to go beyond outcome-only reward signals.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B, 32B), with consistent improvements over a large set of strong, recent open-source RL-tuned baselines.

Thorough ablation suite covering masking strategy (Appendix E), dependency metric choice (Appendix F), rollout group size (Appendix G), entropy penalty (Appendix D), and the two VPPO components (TAS/TGF) individually, which aids reproducibility and helps isolate design choices.
The qualitative case studies (Appendix L) provide an intuitive, concrete illustration of how the baseline fails geometrically/logically while VPPO's reasoning chain is more consistent.

Training dynamics analysis (Figure 5) and the discovery/characterization of policy collapse with uniform rewards (Appendix D) are a useful practical contribution for the community, independent of the main method.
weaknesses: The theoretical variance-reduction result (Theorem 3.1) rests on strong and largely unrealistic assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, independence between advantage and gradients, independence between the shaping factor and advantage, and a 'second-moment dominance' approximation for variance). The derivation is more a stylized heuristic than a rigorous guarantee, and it ignores the bias introduced by discarding 60% of token gradients and reweighting advantages, so the practical implications of the 'theorem' are unclear and somewhat oversold as a formal result.

The core visual-dependency metric is validated only qualitatively (a single annotated example in Fig. 7) and via downstream accuracy; there is no direct validation against an independent notion of ground-truth visual grounding (e.g., human annotation, attention/gaze data), so it remains unclear whether the metric truly captures 'perceptually pivotal' tokens versus simply correlating with easier-to-fit high-information tokens.

Ablation results show diminishing or inconsistent marginal benefit from combining TAS+TGF versus TGF alone (Table 2: TGF-only actually beats full VPPO on MMK12 and MathVision), and the masking-strategy ablation (Table 7) shows only ~1% spread across four very different perturbation types, which weakens the narrative that the specific, principled design choices (versus simpler alternatives) are what drive the gains.

Several 7B baselines are 'reproduced' by the authors (marked with †) using author-provided prompts, and the evaluation pipeline, prompt template, and entropy-penalty tuning are all controlled by the authors; given that no seed variance or confidence intervals are reported for any table, it is hard to assess whether the reported gains (often only 1-3 points over the best baseline, e.g., PAPO-D) are statistically meaningful.

VPPO requires an additional forward pass per rollout (masked image) to compute token dependency scores and introduces three extra hyperparameters (k, βmin, βmax) plus a masking hyperparameter, increasing both computational and tuning complexity; the claimed 10% training-time overhead seems low given the described double-rollout pipeline and is not broken down in detail (e.g., memory footprint of storing two distributions per token).

The entropy penalty (introduced to prevent the DAPO baseline from collapsing) is applied to both the baseline and VPPO for a 'fair' comparison, but this is a nonstandard addition relative to how these baselines are typically trained/reported elsewhere, raising the possibility that the baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples with the original published baseline numbers.

The paper's core claims of novelty ('first attempt' at token perception, 'first multimodal RL algorithm' to identify pivotal tokens) are somewhat overstated given closely related prior work on perception-aware RL (PAPO, already a baseline) and token-level pivotal/critical-token selection in LLM RL (cited in related work), making the incremental technical contribution feel narrower than advertised.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated perspective on multimodal RLVR: the paper introduces token-level 'visual dependency' as a lens to analyze CoT reasoning, supported by clear empirical analyses (Insight 1: sparsity of pivotal tokens; Insight 2: heterogeneity of trajectory-level grounding) that provide a coherent narrative motivating the method.

The proposed VPPO method is simple, interpretable, and principled: combining macro-level trajectory advantage shaping with micro-level sparse gradient masking, and can be plugged into existing GRPO/DAPO-style pipelines.

Extensive empirical validation across eight diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B, 32B), with consistent and often substantial improvements over strong open-source RL-tuned baselines (DAPO, PAPO-D, MM-Eureka, NoisyRollout, etc.).

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise (TAS vs TGF), sensitivity to filtering ratio k and shaping range, comparison against alternative token-selection heuristics (entropy, random), and comparison of dependency-calculation metrics (KL vs JSD vs Top-1 drop) and masking strategies, which collectively strengthen confidence in the design choices.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, training procedure pseudocode, and appendix sections addressing entropy-penalty stabilization, dataset/benchmark analysis, and qualitative case studies contrasting VPPO vs. baseline failure modes.
Training dynamics analysis (faster convergence, more stable training) adds practical value beyond raw accuracy gains.
weaknesses: The theoretical variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 3.1) rests on several strong and somewhat unrealistic assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, independence between advantage and shaping factor/gradients, second-moment dominance); it is more illustrative than a rigorous guarantee and its practical relevance is unclear.

The core visual-dependency metric (KL divergence between original vs. masked-image output distributions) is conceptually similar to established occlusion-based/saliency interpretability techniques, so the technical novelty of the metric itself is somewhat incremental relative to its application in the RL objective.

Computing token-level dependency requires an additional forward pass per rollout with a masked image, adding non-trivial overhead; while the paper reports ~10% training-time increase for 7B, scalability and overhead at even larger scales or with larger rollout groups is not thoroughly analyzed.

The stochastic nature of the random patch-masking strategy used to compute dependency scores could introduce variance into the training signal (different masks yield different KL scores), but the paper does not report variance across multiple mask samples/seeds or multiple training runs for main results.

Several baseline numbers are noted as 'reproductions' using author-provided prompts, which could introduce inconsistencies when comparing against officially reported numbers, and no statistical significance testing is provided for the reported gains.
Some benchmark-level improvements are marginal (e.g., MMK12, DynaMath) and the paper does not discuss why gains vary so much across benchmarks or where VPPO might not help.

The abstract/intro language ('pioneering exploration', 'first attempt') is somewhat overstated given that pivotal-token identification and perception-aware rewards have been explored in related text-only and multimodal RL works (as acknowledged in related work).

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated perspective for multimodal RLVR: quantifying token-level 'visual dependency' via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on original vs. perturbed (masked) visual input, and using this signal to shape both trajectory-level advantages (TAS) and token-level gradient masks (TGF).

Extensive empirical validation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B and 32B), consistently outperforming strong open-source RL-tuned baselines (DAPO, GRPO, MM-Eureka, VL-Rethinker, PAPO, NoisyRollout, etc.).

Very thorough ablation studies: TAS vs. TGF individually and combined; sensitivity to filtering ratio k and shaping range; comparison of dependency-calculation metrics (KL vs JSD vs Top-1 prob drop); comparison of masking/perturbation strategies (patch blackening vs noise vs blur vs full masking); binary vs soft masks; advantage vs reward shaping; generalization to GRPO as base algorithm; rollout group size; entropy-penalty stabilization analysis; and out-of-domain VQA generalization.

Provides a theoretical variance-reduction argument (Theorem 3.1) connecting the sparsity ratio and shaping factor to reduced gradient variance, complementing the empirical training-stability observations.

Good transparency/reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, training procedure pseudocode, computational overhead analysis (only ~10% extra cost) including an equal-time-budget comparison showing gains are not simply due to extra compute, and qualitative case studies contrasting VPPO with baseline failure modes.

The insights (sparse token-level visual dependency; heterogeneous trajectory-level visual grounding) are intuitively appealing and well-illustrated with qualitative examples, providing interpretability alongside performance gains.
weaknesses: The theoretical variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 3.1) relies on several strong, unrealistic independence assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, advantage independent of gradients, dependency independent of advantage), so the 'proof' is more of a rough intuition-building exercise than a rigorous guarantee.

The core dependency metric is based on KL divergence between original and masked-image output distributions; this conflates true visual grounding with generic sensitivity to any large, potentially out-of-distribution perturbation to the input (masked images may look unnatural to the model), which is not fully disentangled despite the masking-strategy ablation.

Some benchmark-level results are mixed rather than uniformly improved (e.g., MMK12 and DynaMath at 32B scale are essentially on par with or slightly below DAPO), which is somewhat understated in the narrative that emphasizes uniform superiority.

Baseline numbers for many competitors are self-reported reproductions (marked with †) rather than official published numbers, raising some concern about comparison fairness, although this is a common and largely unavoidable practice.

Experiments are limited to a single training dataset (ViRL39K) and to reasoning-centric benchmarks; applicability to other data distributions or more subjective/creative multimodal tasks (as the authors themselves note) is untested.

Scaling is only validated up to 32B; behavior at larger scales (e.g., 70B+) remains unverified, and the hyperparameters (k, β range, masking probability) appear tuned specifically to this setup, requiring re-tuning for new settings.

strengths: The core idea of quantifying token-level 'visual dependency' via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on the original vs. a perturbed (masked) image is a reasonably clean and interpretable way to operationalize visual grounding at the token level, and the paper uses it consistently for both trajectory-level advantage shaping and token-level gradient filtering.

The experimental protocol is broad: results are reported on 8 benchmarks spanning math, geometry, logic and multi-discipline reasoning, at both 7B and 32B scale, with a fairly complete set of ablations (masking strategy, dependency metric choice, rollout group size, binary vs. soft mask, reward vs. advantage shaping, entropy penalty, generalization to GRPO, OOD VQA transfer, equal-compute-budget comparison, computational overhead).

The method is simple to integrate into existing RLVR pipelines (plugs into GRPO/DAPO with two extra signals) and the paper provides a full training algorithm, hyperparameters, and claims to release code, supporting reproducibility.

The equal time-budget comparison (Appendix J) that extends DAPO training time to match VPPO's overhead is a good control that helps rule out the trivial explanation that gains come purely from extra compute.
weaknesses: The central 'insights' (visual dependency is sparse across tokens; trajectories differ in overall visual groundedness) are intuitively unsurprising and largely confirmatory rather than genuinely novel scientific findings; similar token-importance/forking-token ideas already exist in the text-only RLVR literature, and perception-aware rewards for LVLMs (e.g., PAPO, cited in the paper) already address closely related issues, undercutting the 'first to study token perception' novelty claim.

The theoretical variance-reduction result (Theorem 3.1) relies on strong, not clearly justified assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, advantage independent of gradients, dependency independent of advantage, roughly constant per-step squared gradient norm) and only shows that restricting the sum to fewer terms and scaling by a bounded factor shrinks the second moment of the estimator — a close-to-tautological statement that does not account for the bias introduced by discarding gradient information from non-pivotal tokens, so the claimed 'lower-variance, better' narrative is not rigorously supported.

Many ablation gaps are small and not accompanied by variance/seed information despite using avg@8 accuracy at temperature 1.0 (a noisy metric), making it hard to assess whether differences such as 57.5 vs 57.1 (TAS+TGF vs TGF-only) or the various masking/metric ablations (±0.5–1 points) are statistically meaningful; the combination of TAS+TGF does not strictly dominate TGF-only on several individual benchmarks (e.g., DynaMath, MathVision), which is not discussed.

Baseline comparisons in the main table mix results reproduced by the authors with numbers from differing original papers/training recipes (different datasets, epochs, max lengths, entropy penalties), which weakens the controlled nature of the 'state-of-the-art' comparison; the fairest controlled comparisons are really only the internal GRPO/DAPO-vs-VPPO ablations.

The computational overhead analysis seems understated relative to the described procedure (a full extra forward pass per trajectory over a masked image for KL computation at every token), and details on how this is batched/amortized are thin; similarly, the perturbation-based dependency metric inherits known issues of counterfactual masking methods (sensitivity to the specific masking distribution, as the paper's own ablation on masking strategies shows only modest but somewhat arbitrary differences).

Qualitative analysis (Figure 7, Appendix O) is based on a small number of cherry-picked examples rather than systematic/quantitative verification that the identified 'pivotal tokens' align with human-judged visual grounding, so the interpretability claims are only weakly substantiated.

Key hyperparameters (k=0.4, beta_min=0.9, dynamic beta_max) appear tuned specifically on the evaluation suite with no demonstrated transfer to new datasets/domains, and the paper's own limitations section concedes this sensitivity, raising concerns about generalizability beyond the tested setup.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely underexplored perspective for multimodal RLVR: quantifying token-level visual dependency via KL divergence between original and perturbed-image output distributions, and using this to motivate two concrete mechanisms (trajectory-level advantage shaping and token-level gradient filtering).

Comprehensive empirical validation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, geometry, logic, multi-discipline) and two model scales (7B, 32B), with consistent and often substantial gains over strong RLVR baselines (DAPO, GRPO, and several recent open-source methods).

Very thorough ablation suite: component-wise ablation (TAS vs TGF), sensitivity to filtering ratio k and shaping range, comparison of masking strategies, comparison of dependency metrics (KL vs JSD vs Top-1 drop), comparison to entropy-based token selection, binary vs soft masking, advantage vs reward shaping, rollout group size, and an equal-compute-budget comparison — this is unusually extensive for a method paper.

Demonstrates generality by applying VPPO on top of GRPO (not just DAPO), and shows positive transfer to out-of-domain VQA benchmarks, suggesting the gains are not merely benchmark-specific overfitting.

Provides an interpretable qualitative case study (Figure 7, Appendix O) showing that high-dependency tokens align with semantically meaningful visual/logical anchors, and side-by-side comparisons with baseline failure modes that are illustrative of the claimed mechanism.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: full hyperparameter tables, training procedure pseudocode, and a code repository are provided.
weaknesses: No variance/seed analysis is reported anywhere in the main results or ablations; RL training is known to be high-variance, and single-run comparisons (especially for close-margin ablations like soft vs. binary mask or advantage vs. reward shaping, which differ by <1.5%) make it hard to assess whether reported improvements are statistically meaningful rather than noise.

The theoretical variance-reduction analysis (Theorem 3.1) relies on several strong, somewhat unrealistic independence assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, independence of advantage and shaping factor from gradients) and ultimately shows a fairly mechanical/tautological result (restricting to a k-fraction of tokens and scaling by a bounded factor reduces the second moment) rather than establishing that this reduced-variance estimator is actually a better or less biased estimator of the true policy gradient.

The visual dependency metric depends on an explicit choice of image perturbation (random patch blackening); while an ablation is provided, the perturbed image is inherently out-of-distribution for the model, so the measured KL divergence may partly reflect OOD sensitivity rather than 'true' visual grounding — this conflation is not analyzed or discussed.

Several baseline numbers in the main table are the authors' own reproductions (marked with †), which introduces potential reproduction bias; it is unclear whether the same level of hyperparameter tuning effort (e.g., entropy penalty coefficient, chosen specifically via ablation on the DAPO baseline) was applied evenly to all competing methods.

The entropy-penalty analysis (Appendix E) reveals that both the baseline and VPPO require a carefully tuned regularizer to avoid catastrophic policy collapse; this raises a question about whether the reported DAPO baseline is somewhat under-tuned/fragile relative to what could be achieved with more careful stabilization, and whether VPPO's advantage would narrow under a better-tuned baseline.

The core idea of identifying 'pivotal tokens' for sparse gradient updates is a direct multimodal adaptation of prior text-only work on high-entropy/forking tokens (Wang et al., 2025c) and critical-token contrastive estimation (Lin et al., 2024); while the visual-dependency framing is a reasonable and seemingly effective adaptation, the degree of conceptual novelty beyond combining known reward-shaping and gradient-masking ideas with a new scoring signal is somewhat incremental.

The paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations of VPPO's own mechanism (e.g., scenarios where visual dependency may be a poor proxy for reasoning quality, or trajectories where masking fails to produce a meaningful distributional shift), limiting the completeness of the analysis.
